rows.notes: The cited document is the UN World Water Development Report 2022 (UNESCO/UN-Water), a global synthesis/assessment report compiled from literature, agency statistics (Aquastat etc.) and contributed boxes; it reports no original experiment, survey or model runs of its own. It is a review-type document, so Q1 is 'no'. The report does not discuss microirrigation or drip irrigation beyond a passing mention of micro-irrigation as a water-conservation measure in the Rajasthan MJSA programme (Section 8.4.4); it contains no evidence on microirrigation enhancing soil quality, water quality, farmer prices, input costs, or public investment in agriculture. The claim attributed to this source is not supported by its content.

Same document: a UN synthesis report (WWDR 2022) on groundwater, not a primary study, so Q1 is 'no'. It does not report any own result on microirrigation or drip irrigation conferring crop resistance to climate change; the only drip/microirrigation reference is a brief mention of micro-irrigation promoted under Rajasthan's MJSA groundwater recharge programme (Section 8.4.4), cited from Verma and Shah (2019). Climate-resilience content in the report concerns groundwater storage and managed aquifer recharge, not irrigation technology.

notes: The cited document is the full text of the UN World Water Development Report 2022 'Groundwater: Making the invisible visible'.
